query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor amount of aluminum (≈3 at%) into equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will enable the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent alumina scale during high‐temperature exposure, thereby significantly improving its oxidation resistance without substantially degrading its room‐ or high‐temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy, exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding approximately 3 atomic percent aluminum during melting/casting (with proportional adjustment of other constituents) to enable alumina scale formation.
generation.conditions: Test under an air atmosphere at 800 °C for a 5-hour exposure. Mechanical properties should be examined at room temperature and at high temperature (near 1000 °C) under similar strain rates (10^−4–10^−2 s^−1) as the untreated alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, protective Al2O3 (alumina) layer on the alloy surface which acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
generation.mechanism: The minor Al addition is expected to segregate to the surface during high-temperature exposure, where it oxidizes preferentially to form an alumina scale. This scale has low oxygen diffusivity, thereby reducing further oxidation of the underlying alloy while preserving the overall microstructure that imparts desirable mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-doped alloy will show markedly reduced oxidation (e.g., lower weight gain and thinner, more adherent oxide scales) compared to untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr under the same exposure conditions, while maintaining similar room- and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which exhibits rapid oxidation (pesting) in air at 800 °C over 5 hours, with no significant protective scale formation.
generation.boundary: The benefits are predicted for exposures in air at temperatures near 800 °C for time durations around 5 hours, and for mechanical testing conditions similar to those previously reported (room temperature ductility of 8–16% and yield strengths of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum content for scale formation without compromising intrinsic mechanical properties is not fully established, and there may be trade-offs between oxidation resistance and potential changes in phase stability or ductility that require experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two cohorts of samples: one of standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and one of the modified alloy with ≈3 at% aluminum (adjusted composition). Subject both cohorts to an air atmosphere at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, perform mass gain measurements, microstructural characterization (using SEM, EDS, and XRD to assess scale formation), and tensile testing at room temperature and at high temperature (≈1000 °C) at strain rates between 10^−4 and 10^−2 s^−1.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area (to quantify oxidation rate)
Phase composition of the scale (confirmation of Al2O3 formation)
Tensile properties (ductility and yield strength) before and after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (i.e., similar mass gain and oxide scale characteristics to the untreated alloy) or if its room- or high-temperature mechanical properties degrade beyond acceptable margins relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.
